tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

schema.name: Write
schema.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

4	[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#custommd)). Loaded last. On conflict, this file wins.

22	  - Fetch: at an acquaint and at every cycle start the session does that README's Fetch action

1	# Contributing
2	
3	How to build, test, and change vc-x1, for a person or an agent. What vc-x1 is, and how to install
4	and use it, is in [README.md](README.md). How a change is made, the cycle and its commits, is in
5	[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol).
6	
7	## Tasks
8	
9	The project's tasks, in the order a change uses them. A change is made as a
10	[cycle](AGENTS.md#terminology): one commit, or a ladder of commits each called a rung, made on a
11	bookmark of its own and joined to `main` at the end, the Land. A task is named by its first column,
12	the name the agent-files use for it.
13	
14	- Dev and release: the dev build is the quick debug one, for trying a change while it is made, and
15	  the release build is the optimized one installed as `vc-x1` at Land.
16	- The commands are the workspace's own `cargo xtask`, the `xtask/` package, which needs nothing
17	  installed: `cargo xtask -h` lists its tasks, and `cargo xtask completions` explains the shell
18	  alias, `cx` here, and its completion. Its settings are `Cargo.toml`'s
19	  `[workspace.metadata.xtask]`.
20	
21	| Task | What it does | When | Command |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| bump | sets the version in `Cargo.toml` and refreshes `Cargo.lock`, `X.Y.Z-N` for a cycle's Nth commit and the bare `X.Y.Z` for its last ([Suffix scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)) | first, at each commit of a cycle | `cargo xtask bump next`, or `bump X.Y.Z` |
24	| validate | formats the code, runs the lints, and runs every test, the fixture tests included | before each review, and before every commit | `cargo xtask validate` |
25	| validate fast | runs the binaries' unit tests only, changing no file | while a review iterates | `cargo xtask validate --fast` |
26	| test | builds and runs the tests named | to run one test, or the tests matching a filter | `cargo test [<filter>]` |
27	| clippy | runs the lints, a warning failing it | to see the lints alone | `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` |
28	| build | builds the dev binary, `target/debug/vc-x1`, with the commit it was built from | to build the change without running it | `cargo xtask build` |
29	| run | builds the dev binary, then runs it with the arguments, no `--` needed | to try the change | `cargo xtask run <args>` |
30	| install | builds the dev binary, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1-dev`, beside the installed `vc-x1` | after each rung's commit, and to try the change from any directory | `cargo xtask install` |
31	| install release | builds the release binary and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1`, printing its version | at Land | `cargo xtask install --release` |
32	
33	Each building task takes `--release` or `--profile NAME`, a `Cargo.toml` profile, dev by default,
34	and `--bin NAME` for another binary. vc-x1's own `validate`, `build`, `run`, and `install` are
35	deprecated, each warning and naming its task, and a later release refuses them.
36	
37	## Agents
38	
39	What an agent working here reads beyond the agent-files, read at acquaint after `custom.md`
40	([Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint)). It is the project's layer over the agent-files, committed, so
41	every clone has it, and a workspace's `custom.md`, local and gitignored, overrides it.
42	
43	- Agent-files: vc-x1's are the `v0.3.1-18` draft of `### agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1` in
44	  [TODO.md](TODO.md), adopted locally (2026-11-03, `-1` and `-2` 2026-11-04, `-8` to `-10`
45	  2026-11-11, `-11` to `-13` 2026-11-13, `-14` and `-15` 2026-11-16, `-16` 2026-11-18, `-17`
46	  2026-11-21, `-18` 2026-11-25). The proposal stays open, to be made formal by the next cycle.
47	- Messaging: the projects of the family message each other through the `../vc-x1-messages` repo,
48	  beside the work-repo, a clone of `https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1-messages.git`. A
49	  workspace without it clones it there. Its `README.md` is the protocol and it governs.
50	  - At an acquaint and at every cycle start the session does that README's Fetch action first,
51	    under its guards, and at acquaint reads what is pending for us, per its Read messages action.
52	  - A Fetch is asked for unless the workspace's `custom.md` gives a standing permission.

content.content:
## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

vc-x1 0.85.27+cd95ea775573

A cycle's stages, each a subcommand, beside `rung`'s acts: `plan
start` makes the bookmark and writes the record, `plan commit`
commits the plan, the opening, `rung next` and `rung commit` run
each work rung, `close` makes the
closing, `squash` makes the cycle one commit instead, `land` lands
it on a target, and `push` publishes what the
cycle's state calls for. `ladder` rewrites zTOC.md's ladder from the
rung headings, and `status` says where the cycle stands. A later
stage chains as a flag, `cycle close --land main --push`.

The version is the project's, and no stage writes it, `rung next
--ver` running the config's `[version] bump`. -R is optional and
says where, a workspace or a plain repo.

Usage: vc-x1 cycle [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  plan    Plan a cycle: `start` makes the bookmark and the record, `commit`
          commits the plan
  ladder  Make zTOC.md's ladder from the rung headings in TODO.md
  status  Say where the cycle stands, changing nothing
  close   Close a ladder: its closing commit, made from the work `@`
  squash  Make the cycle one commit: its rungs and the work `@` squashed into
          the opening
  land    Land the closed cycle on TARGET
  push    Publish what the cycle's state calls for
  help    Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

vc-x1-dev 0.85.28+c36f0da74fcf.dirty

Start a cycle's plan: make the bookmark on the work @ first, the
slug of --title or --bookmark's name, kept local, then write the
cycle's record. In TODO.md what `## Closed` holds is deleted and the
`## Todo` entry titled as --title is moved into an `## In Progress`
scaffold, an empty one when no entry matches, and in zTOC.md the
ladder is replaced with the opening and the closing. A workspace with
no TODO.md or no zTOC.md gets a skeleton of the file first, the
headings the record needs, and a file there is kept. Every check is
made before anything changes: a cycle in progress is refused, as is
a name in use. --no-record makes the bookmark alone, writing no
file, a branch the later stages will not take, as does --bookmark
without --title. With --ver the opening's version is set last, by
the config's `[version] bump`, so the plan under review carries it.
Nothing is committed or pushed.

Usage: vc-x1-dev cycle plan start [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --title <STR>
          The bare cycle title, a Conventional Commit: the bookmark is its slug,
          and the record is written under it

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --no-record
          Make the bookmark alone and write no record

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --ver <VERSION>
          The opening's version, set by the config's `[version] bump` once the
          record is written [default: the version left as it is]

      --bookmark [<NAME>]
          The cycle's bookmark, in place of the title's slug; bare, with `rung
          commit --title`, the title's slug made or moved for it

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace, its root or either repo, or a plain
          repo [default: the current directory]

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

60	## Todo format
61	
62	`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
63	reference links to more detail.
64	
65	- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
66	  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
67	  agent that reads it, after filing each fact into its home or keeping the bullet whose fact has
68	  none, so a reset never destroys the only copy of anything.
69	- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
70	- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
71	  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
72	- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
73	  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
74	- `## Ideas`: unranked.
75	- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
76	- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
77	- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference
78	  numbering](#reference-numbering)).
79	
80	Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
81	project's record, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
82	`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.
83	
84	An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
85	entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
86	is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
87	verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
88	renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
89	form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
90	bold title, cited by the bold text.
91	
92	Example shape:
93	
94	```
95	## Todo
96	
97	### Add new feature X
98	
99	The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).
100	
101	### Fix bug Y
102	
103	What is wrong and where [[1]].
104	
105	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
106	```
107	
108	## The In Progress block
109	
110	A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
111	([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
112	deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
113	item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
114	required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
115	other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
116	under a program heading, each one deeper):
117	
118	- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
119	- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
120	- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
121	  body carries the final one
122	- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
123	  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
124	  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
125	- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
126	  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
127	  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
128	  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
129	  answer
130	- **rungs**: a `#### Rungs` heading over the rung subsections, the ladder itself being `zTOC.md`'s
131	  ([zTOC format](#ztoc-format)), made by the tool from the subsections' headings, so a rung is
132	  written once, as its heading: one rung per step, `- 2 (done) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)`: the
133	  rung's number, its position in the ladder from `0`, then the marker, `(done)` or `(current)`, both
134	  first so they read down their columns, and a rung not yet started has neither, and an inline link
135	  so the ladder is one list with nothing beside it to keep in step, its line as long as the title
136	  makes it. A rung is `(done)` when a commit of its title is on the cycle's branch, and `(current)`
137	  when `rung next` started it and no commit has ended it, a marker of the working copy alone that no

## Todo format

`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
reference links to more detail.

- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
  agent that reads it, after filing each fact into its home or keeping the bullet whose fact has
  none, so a reset never destroys the only copy of anything.
- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
- `## Ideas`: unranked.
- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference
  numbering](#reference-numbering)).

Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
project's record, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.

An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
bold title, cited by the bold text.

Example shape:

```
## Todo

### Add new feature X

The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).

### Fix bug Y

What is wrong and where [[1]].

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
```

## The In Progress block

A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
under a program heading, each one deeper):

- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
  body carries the final one
- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
  answer
- **rungs**: a `#### Rungs` heading over the rung subsections, the ladder itself being `zTOC.md`'s
  ([zTOC format](#ztoc-format)), made by the tool from the subsections' headings, so a rung is
  written once, as its heading: one rung per step, `- 2 (done) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)`: the
  rung's number, its position in the ladder from `0`, then the marker, `(done)` or `(current)`, both
  first so they read down their columns, and a rung not yet started has neither, and an inline link
  so the ladder is one list with nothing beside it to keep in step, its line as long as the title
  makes it. A rung is `(done)` when a commit of its title is on the cycle's branch, and `(current)`
  when `rung next` started it and no commit has ended it, a marker of the working copy alone that no
  commit carries, so no marker is typed. `<title>` is the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per
  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a `## Todo`
  entry is retitled as its cycle title before `cycle plan start` moves it. The first rung is `<cycle
  title> opening` and the last `<cycle title> closing`, linked like the rest

`#### Rungs` holds the **rung subsections**, one per rung in the ladder's order, the closing
included, headed by the rung's exact title, so the ladder is their index. Each opens at laddering
with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and
completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals,
never a restatement of the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out
the cycle." and completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or
`_None._`.

A rung is `- N (marker) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title
links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- N (marker) <cycle title>`, with no subsection
under it: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

## zTOC format

`zTOC.md`, beside `TODO.md` at the work-repo root, is the workspace's index, so the running ladder
and the files worth knowing are found without reading `TODO.md`'s length, and the `z` sorts it last
in a listing. Its sections, in this order:

- `# TOC`, the title.
- `## Ladder`: the cycle's ladder, its one copy, each rung with its marker as [The In Progress
  block](#the-in-progress-block) shapes it, linking across to its subsection in `TODO.md`, since a
  same-file link does not work in every markdown preview, zed's among them. Written by `vc-x1
  cycle plan start`, replacing the last cycle's, made again from the rung headings by `cycle ladder`
  and by every cycle commit, and kept by the closing commit, so the landmark's tree holds the
  finished ladder beside its `## Closed`. Its grammar is strict: each rung a left-margin `- `
  line, and the tool refuses to rewrite a ladder holding any other line but a blank one.
- `## The TOC`: one link per file worth knowing, with what it holds, `TODO.md` first, its line
  linking the todo list as well, `[todo list](TODO.md#todo)`, so the Todos are one step away.

Its links are inline, so it has no `# References`.

Like `TODO.md` it is not an agent-file, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton, `##
Ladder` reading `_None._` until the first opening.

60	## Todo format
61	
62	`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
63	reference links to more detail.
64	
65	- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
66	  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
67	  agent that reads it, after filing each fact into its home or keeping the bullet whose fact has
68	  none, so a reset never destroys the only copy of anything.
69	- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
70	- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
71	  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
72	- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
73	  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
74	- `## Ideas`: unranked.
75	- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
76	- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
77	- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference
78	  numbering](#reference-numbering)).
79	
80	Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
81	project's record, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
82	`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.
83	
84	An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
85	entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
86	is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
87	verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
88	renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
89	form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
90	bold title, cited by the bold text.
91	
92	Example shape:
93	
94	```
95	## Todo
96	
97	### Add new feature X
98	
99	The feature, in a sentence or two ([details](features.md#feature-x)).
100	
101	### Fix bug Y
102	
103	What is wrong and where [[1]].
104	
105	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
106	```
107	
108	## The In Progress block
109	
110	A cycle's record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, written at the opening
111	([Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), finalized and moved to `## Closed` by the closing commit, and
112	deleted by the next opening ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). The picked-up `## Todo`
113	item is moved here (never copied) and becomes the cycle-record's **provisional items**, all
114	required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the
115	other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and
116	under a program heading, each one deeper):
117	
118	- **title**, the cycle's name, what `git log --grep` finds it by
119	- **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
120	- **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad. Provisional, and the close-out's commit
121	  body carries the final one
122	- **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?", specific enough that a reader can run
123	  it. Not the per-commit validation, which asks whether the artifact still works. A changed check is
124	  one of the things the deliberation exists to justify
125	- **deliberation**: how the other five were decided, one bullet per decision. The bullet's lead
126	  names the decision and its sentence states it, and the sub-bullets carry the reasons, the
127	  alternatives weighed, and the costs accepted, so a reader can skim the decisions and read the
128	  reasons only where they doubt one. `_None._` when there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real
129	  answer
130	- **rungs**: a `#### Rungs` heading over the rung subsections, the ladder itself being `zTOC.md`'s
131	  ([zTOC format](#ztoc-format)), made by the tool from the subsections' headings, so a rung is
132	  written once, as its heading: one rung per step, `- 2 (done) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)`: the
133	  rung's number, its position in the ladder from `0`, then the marker, `(done)` or `(current)`, both
134	  first so they read down their columns, and a rung not yet started has neither, and an inline link
135	  so the ladder is one list with nothing beside it to keep in step, its line as long as the title
136	  makes it. A rung is `(done)` when a commit of its title is on the cycle's branch, and `(current)`
137	  when `rung next` started it and no commit has ended it, a marker of the working copy alone that no
138	  commit carries, so no marker is typed. `<title>` is the rung's commit title, `<type>: <desc>` per
139	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit), so a `## Todo`
140	  entry is retitled as its cycle title before `cycle plan start` moves it. The first rung is `<cycle
141	  title> opening` and the last `<cycle title> closing`, linked like the rest
142	
143	`#### Rungs` holds the **rung subsections**, one per rung in the ladder's order, the closing
144	included, headed by the rung's exact title, so the ladder is their index. Each opens at laddering
145	with an abstract-sized intent statement (the rung's problem and solution in a sentence or two) and
146	completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals,
147	never a restatement of the landed commit body. The closing rung's opens with the stub "Closing out
148	the cycle." and completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or
149	`_None._`.
150	
151	A rung is `- N (marker) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title
152	links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's [Steps are named, not
153	numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)), so a title carries no number, no version, and no
154	SHA. The version-of-record still bumps for every rung and its suffix still encodes the stage, but
155	that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.
156	
157	A single-step cycle's ladder is one unlinked rung, `- N (marker) <cycle title>`, with no subsection
158	under it: a subsection headed by the title would collide with the title heading's anchor ([Cycle
159	shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
160	
161	The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
162	`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
163	
164	## zTOC format
165	
166	`zTOC.md`, beside `TODO.md` at the work-repo root, is the workspace's index, so the running ladder
167	and the files worth knowing are found without reading `TODO.md`'s length, and the `z` sorts it last
168	in a listing. Its sections, in this order:
169	
170	- `# TOC`, the title.
171	- `## Ladder`: the cycle's ladder, its one copy, each rung with its marker as [The In Progress
172	  block](#the-in-progress-block) shapes it, linking across to its subsection in `TODO.md`, since a
173	  same-file link does not work in every markdown preview, zed's among them. Written by `vc-x1
174	  cycle plan start`, replacing the last cycle's, made again from the rung headings by `cycle ladder`
175	  and by every cycle commit, and kept by the closing commit, so the landmark's tree holds the
176	  finished ladder beside its `## Closed`. Its grammar is strict: each rung a left-margin `- `
177	  line, and the tool refuses to rewrite a ladder holding any other line but a blank one.
178	- `## The TOC`: one link per file worth knowing, with what it holds, `TODO.md` first, its line
179	  linking the todo list as well, `[todo list](TODO.md#todo)`, so the Todos are one step away.
180	
181	Its links are inline, so it has no `# References`.
182	
183	Like `TODO.md` it is not an agent-file, and `scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh` ships it as a skeleton, `##
184	Ladder` reading `_None._` until the first opening.

135:## Suffix scheme
136-
137-The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
138-encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
139-Preparation**.
140-
141-This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
142-a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
143-number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
144-The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.
145-
146-- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
147-- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
148-- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
149-
150-**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
151-starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
152-bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
153-needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
154-step without renumbering siblings.
155-
156-Disambiguation:
157-
158-- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
159-- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
160-
161-**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

Create a project, a dual workspace or a plain repo with -s por

Usage: vc-x1-dev init [OPTIONS] [TARGET]

Arguments:
  [TARGET]
          What to create: URL, path, or bare NAME, the one positional.
          
          - URL: `git@host:owner/name(.git)?`, `https://...(.git)?`,
            used as-is, config not consulted.
          - Path: `./X`, `../X`, `/X`, `~/X`, `~`, `.`, `..`, is the
            directory path, remote resolved via `--repo` chain.
          - Bare NAME: becomes NAME.git, remote resolved via
            `--repo` chain.
          
          A slashed target with no path prefix (`owner/name`) is
          refused: it reads equally as a path and as the retired
          owner/name shorthand, so pass `./owner/name` or a URL.

Options:
  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --test-repo <REMOTES>
          Make the target a throwaway test repo, its bare remotes in
          REMOTES, so nothing leaves this machine.
          
          The remotes are named by the repo, `<name>.git` and
          `<name>.agent-session.git`, so several test repos share one
          REMOTES, and a name already there is refused. REMOTES is
          always a path, so `tmp/remotes` needs no `./`. Not with a URL
          target, or what names a remote. With `--adopt` the target
          is an existing repo or directory, an origin it has replaced by
          REMOTES and kept only by `--upstream`.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --name <NAME>
          Repo directory name override (URL form only).
          
          - URL form: repo created at `cwd/<NAME>` instead of the
            URL-derived name.
          - Path / bare-NAME forms: error if given (TARGET already
            names the repo).

      --account <NAME>
          Account name: picks `[account.<a>]` from user config.
          
          - Without this flag, `[default].account` (or top-level
            `[repo]` shorthand) is used.
          - Meaningful only with Path or bare-NAME targets, since a
            URL target supplies the remote directly.

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --repo <CAT[=VAL]>
          Repo target: `<cat>` or `<cat>=<val>`.
          
          - `<cat>` looks up the value via the account chain
            in the user config.
          - `<cat>=<val>` uses the literal value, no config
            lookup needed.
          - Specific category meanings (`remote`, `local`,
            ...) depend on the consumer subcommand.

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          What to create, `b|both` a dual workspace (work + agent repo) or
          `p|por` a plain single repo [default: both]
          
          [possible values: both, por]

          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

      --private
          Create private GitHub repos (default: public).

            `gh repo create` (GitHub URL or `--repo remote` whose
            value points at GitHub).

      --push-retries <PUSH_RETRIES>
          Max push retries after repo creation [default: 5]
          
          [default: 5]

      --push-retry-delay <PUSH_RETRY_DELAY>
          Seconds between push retries [default: 3]
          
          [default: 3]

      --config <none|PATH>
          Override the canned workspace config write.
          
          - Absent: write the canned `.vc-config.md`.
          - `--config none`: skip writing entirely.
          - `--config <path>`: copy `<path>` to `.vc-config.md`, or to
            `.vc-config.toml` for a source that is not markdown
            (bytewise; no schema validation).

      --adopt
          Convert an existing TARGET into a dual workspace rather than refuse
          it.
          
          TARGET may be a plain directory, a repo with no workspace config, or a
          single-repo workspace. A dual workspace is refused, having nothing to
          grow.

      --upstream [<NAME>]
          With `--test-repo` and `--adopt`, keep the adopted repo's old
          `origin` as the remote NAME [default NAME: upstream], where it
          is otherwise removed.
          
          The test repo's remotes are REMOTES either way, and nothing
          vc-x1 runs pushes to NAME, so it is there to fetch from. A NAME
          the repo already has is refused.

      --no-url-trailer
          Stamp each initial commit's `ochid:` alone, with no `orepo:` link. A
          plain repo stamps no trailer, so it changes nothing there

      --agent-dir <DIR>
          The agent repo's directory, one name inside the project directory
          [default: .agent-session]. Dual only

      --agent-repo <NAME>
          The agent repo's full name on its remote. Dual only.
          
          Default: the work repo's name plus `--agent-suffix`.

      --agent-suffix <SUFFIX>
          The suffix the work repo's name takes to name the agent repo on its
          remote, beginning with `.` or `-` [default: .agent-session]. Dual only

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

2:# vc-dr-apply.sh: apply a source dual repo's rules and agent files, and its skeletons, as its
3:# working copy holds them or as landed, to a bare dual workspace that `vc-x1 init` made, new or
4:# adopted. It may live anywhere, ~/bin included, since the skeletons come from the source. A
5:# first cut: it writes only new files, refuses when any existing file would change, and commits
6:# nothing.
9:die() {
14:usage() {
17:                      [--lang NAME] [--dry-run] SOURCE [AGENT_SOURCE]
18:       vc-dr-apply.sh --lang [--skel DIR] [SOURCE]
33:  --lang NAME      also apply the language skeleton vc-dr-apply-lang/NAME/, its tasks filled
34:                   into CONTRIBUTING.md; --lang alone lists them
53:gets the source's xtask/ at the same revision, the project's tasks, by `vc-x1 xtask copy`, which
54:adds its member and its `cargo xtask` alias. VC_X1 names the vc-x1 it runs [default: vc-x1].
94:    --lang)
95:        # A language name has no '/', so a path after --lang is the SOURCE to list from.
116:    ((${#sources[@]} || ${#skel_opt})) || die "--lang alone lists from SOURCE or --skel DIR, see --help"
121:# The agent repo a workspace's .vc-config.md names, absolute.
122:agent_of() {
133:# The one commit REV names in REPO, refused unless it is exactly one. A jj command snapshots the
134:# working copy first, so `@` is the tree on disk, and jj keeps its commit in the git store, where
135:# `git archive` reads it.
136:commit_of() {
143:# Whether PATH exists in REPO at SHA.
144:in_commit() {
148:absolute() {
153:# What a revision is, for the plan and the commit body: the working copy by its change id, which
154:# survives the snapshot's rewrites, or the revision as given.
155:named() {
167:# --- The source, and the commit of each repo ---------------------------------------------------
185:# --- The skeletons -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
203:# The language skeletons, one per directory with a tasks.md.
204:langs() {
224:# --- The target workspace ----------------------------------------------------------------------
239:# --- Stage what would be written ---------------------------------------------------------------
244:# Archive the PATHS present in REPO at SHA into DEST.
245:take() {
262:cp -R "$skel/vc-dr-apply-base/work/." "$stage/work/"
269:    cp -R "$lang_dir/." "$stage/work/"
283:# A Rust skeleton gets the source's xtask/, staged at the same revision, for `vc-x1 xtask copy`.
284:xtask_src=
286:    if in_commit "$src" "$sha" xtask/Cargo.toml; then
287:        xtask_src=$tmp/xtask-src

291:        echo "vc-dr-apply: the source has no xtask/ at ${sha:0:12}, so the $lang skeleton gets none"
298:# A path naming {name} or {module} is renamed, the deepest first.
306:# --- The plan ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
312:# Why REL cannot be written under DEST: it, or a directory it needs, is a symlink or the wrong
313:# kind of entry. Empty when it can.
314:blocked() {
332:plan_side() {
358:# xtask/ is `vc-x1 xtask copy`'s to bring, and to bring up to date when it is there.
359:if [[ -n $xtask_src && -e $ws/xtask ]]; then

370:[[ -z $xtask_src ]] ||
371:    echo "  xtask     work xtask/, its Cargo.toml member, and its cargo alias, by \`$vc_x1 xtask copy\`"
381:# --- Apply -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
388:    cp "$stage/$side/$rel" "$dest/$rel"
393:if [[ -n $xtask_src ]]; then

395:        die "the files are written and \`$vc_x1 xtask copy\` failed: \`jj restore\` in $ws undoes it"

7	## Prose form
8	
9	([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
10	
11	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
12	the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
13	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
14	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
15	per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
16	hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
17	relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
18	punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19	
20	Surfaces that use this shape:
21	
22	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
23	  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
25	  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
26	- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
27	  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
28	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
29	  still fine.
30	
31	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32	
33	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, as two
34	  paragraphs by [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
35	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
36	    first and it answers the problem
37	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
38	    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
39	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. What
40	    wants more than a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
41	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
42	    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
43	    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
44	- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
45	  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
46	  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
47	  thinking, and none restates another.
48	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
49	
50	### Leads are labels, unmarked
51	
52	In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
53	the sentence after it is complete without it:
54	
55	```
56	1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
57	```
58	
59	- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
60	  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
61	  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
62	  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
63	  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
64	- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
65	  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
66	  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
67	  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
68	  renumbering.
69	- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
70	  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
71	- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
72	  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
73	  (wink, 2026-08-21).
74	- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.
75	
76	### One spelling per term
77	
78	A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
79	`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
80	spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
81	where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.
82	
83	### Bullet form
84	
85	A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
86	is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
87	the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
88	recast so the name is not the first word.
89	
90	### Line widths
91	
92	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
93	restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
94	when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
95	
96	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
97	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
98	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
99	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
100	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
101	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
102	
103	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
104	touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
105	narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
106	row, indented code in a comment).
107	
108	### Problem-first shape
109	
110	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
111	shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
112	
113	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
114	  follows it.
115	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
116	  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
117	  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
118	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
119	  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
120	    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
121	    `(done)` form.
122	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
123	    into a cycle.
124	
125	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
126	writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
127	body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
128	is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
129	was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
130	opening what it intended to do.
